title: India Just Became the World’s Top Wellness Travel Destination — And the Diaspora Always Knew
excerpt: A new global ranking places India above Thailand, Japan and Switzerland for holistic tourism. For NRIs who grew up with haldi doodh and morning yoga, it’s validation decades in the making.
body:
India has been named the world’s number one wellness travel destination for 2026, overtaking Thailand, Indonesia, Japan, Switzerland and Australia in Travel And Tour World’s annual Top 50 Wellness Destinations ranking published on May 18. For the millions of NRIs who grew up drinking haldi doodh before the wellness industry rebranded it as “golden milk,” the recognition lands somewhere between vindication and a shrug.

## The $35-Billion Homecoming

The ranking reflects a structural shift in global tourism. Industry estimates peg India’s wellness tourism economy at roughly $35 billion in 2025, with projections reaching $116 billion by 2035. Mordor Intelligence forecasts the domestic wellness tourism market growing from $30.95 billion in 2026 to $43.76 billion by 2031, at a compound annual growth rate of 7.18 per cent. These are no longer niche numbers.

What propelled India past its competitors was the depth and authenticity of its offerings. While Bali sells yoga-and-smoothie retreats and Switzerland trades on alpine spa luxury, India’s healing traditions — Ayurveda, yoga, Vedanta, naturopathy, meditation — are woven into a civilisational framework thousands of years old. The difference between a commercial wellness product and a living healthcare system turned out to matter.

## Kerala to Rishikesh: The New Itinerary

Kerala continues to anchor India’s Ayurveda tourism with its Panchakarma detox programmes, herbal therapies and backwater retreats. Rishikesh remains the global epicentre for yoga teacher training and spiritual immersion beside the Ganges. Dharamshala draws mindfulness seekers through Tibetan meditation and Buddhist wellness practices, while Goa’s beachfront retreats cater to the digital detox crowd.

The luxury end is keeping pace. Ananda in the Himalayas — perched in Uttarakhand’s Himalayan foothills — won the 2026 Global Spa Awards for Best Ayurveda Retreat, combining traditional treatments with modern wellness science. Luxury wellness resorts across the country now integrate longevity programmes, biohacking, nutritional therapy and sleep science alongside classical Ayurvedic protocols.

The government’s AYUSH sector is backing the push. International Yoga Day 2026 on June 21 is expected to see record global participation, with pre-celebrations already underway — including a 650-person Common Yoga Protocol session at S-VYASA and a pre-Yoga Day event at the Indian Consulate in Shanghai that underscored yoga’s growing footprint in China.

## Modi’s Nordic Wellness Diplomacy

Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Gothenburg, Sweden, on May 17 added a diplomatic dimension. While the formal agenda centred on trade and innovation, the visit sparked renewed conversations about Ayurveda’s integration into European healthcare. Stina Andersson, chairperson of the Ayurveda Sweden Association, described it as a “major opportunity” for Indian Ayurvedic doctors and therapists to collaborate with Swedish healthcare institutions.

A Swedish delegation had earlier visited the National Institute of Ayurveda in Panchkula to study treatment systems and patient care — part of a broader pattern of European curiosity about India’s preventive healthcare traditions. Andersson floated the idea of integrating Ayurveda with artificial intelligence and nanotechnology to improve accessibility, signalling that the field’s global trajectory is far from purely traditional.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs, this ranking crystallises something they have observed for years: the practices their grandmothers insisted on — turmeric in milk, morning pranayama, seasonal dietary adjustments, oil pulling — are now the foundation of a trillion-dollar global wellness industry.

The more tangible shift is in travel patterns. Increasing numbers of diaspora travellers are combining family visits to India with structured wellness retreats, turning the annual trip home into a Panchakarma-and-parents itinerary. Kerala’s backwater retreats and Rishikesh’s ashrams report growing NRI bookings, particularly from the United States, United Kingdom and Canada, where Ayurveda remains largely unregulated and expensive.

India’s rise to the top of the wellness rankings is not a marketing coup. It is the global market finally catching up to what a fifth of the world’s population has practiced, in one form or another, for millennia. The grandmother’s kitchen was ahead of the curve all along.
